category.title: Game Theory & Adversarial Search
category.description: Impartial & Partisan Games, Winning vs Losing States, Nim Game, Nim-Sum, Sprague-Grundy Theorem, Grundy Numbers (Mex), and Minimax with Alpha-Beta Pruning.

algorithms.title: Winning and Losing States (N-Positions & P-Positions)
algorithms.summary: Classifies game positions into Winning States (N-Positions where Next player wins) and Losing States (P-Positions where Previous player wins).
explanation: 1. Terminal Position: Position with no valid outgoing moves is a Losing State (P-position under normal play).
2. Winning State (N-position): A position is a Winning State if there exists AT LEAST ONE move to a Losing State.
3. Losing State (P-position): A position is a Losing State if ALL valid outgoing moves lead to Winning States.
4. Dynamic Programming / Backward Induction: Evaluate game graph from terminal states backward to classify all positions.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Subtraction Game (Take 1 or 2 stones from N=4)
traceSteps: N=1: Can move to N=0 (P-pos) -> Winning State (N-position).
N=2: Can move to N=0 (P-pos) -> Winning State (N-position).
N=3: Can move to N=1 (N-pos) or N=2 (N-pos) -> All moves lead to N-positions -> Losing State (P-position).
N=4: Can move to N=3 (P-pos) -> Winning State!

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines optimal game outcome (Win or Loss) from any given state.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When analyzing impartial two-player finite games under normal play rules.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Combinatorial game analysis, subtraction games, coin pile games.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Backward induction DP evaluates all reachable states linearly.

algorithms.title: Classic Game of Nim
algorithms.summary: Classic multi-pile impartial game where two players take turns removing any number of objects from a single pile.
explanation: 1. Rules: Given N piles of stones. On a turn, a player chooses one non-empty pile and removes any positive number of stones.
2. Normal Play Convention: The last player to make a move (taking the final stone) wins.
3. Game State Evaluation: If total XOR sum of all pile sizes is non-zero, the first player has a guaranteed winning strategy.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Nim with Piles [3, 4, 5]
traceSteps: XOR sum: 3 ^ 4 ^ 5 = 2 != 0 -> Winning state for Player 1.
Player 1 reduces pile of size 5 to size 3 (since 5 ^ 2 = 7... change pile 3 of size 5 to 3^4^0 = 7? Change pile 1 of 3 to 3^2 = 1).
New piles [1, 4, 5] -> XOR sum = 1 ^ 4 ^ 5 = 0 (Losing state for Player 2!).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines optimal winner in multi-heap stone removal games.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When analyzing impartial games with independent heaps/piles.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Combinatorial game theory, competitive programming heap games.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Single pass O(N) evaluation using Nim-Sum theorem.

algorithms.title: Nim-Sum & XOR Invariant Property
algorithms.summary: Calculates Nim-Sum (bitwise XOR sum of pile sizes) and constructs the optimal winning move.
explanation: 1. Nim-Sum Definition: `S = x1 ^ x2 ^ ... ^ xn`.
2. Winning Invariant: If `S != 0`, there exists at least one pile `x_i` such that `x_i ^ S < x_i`.
3. Optimal Move Strategy: Reduce pile `x_i` to `x_i' = x_i ^ S`. The new Nim-Sum becomes `S' = S ^ x_i ^ x_i' = S ^ x_i ^ (x_i ^ S) = 0`.
4. Opponent's Forced Result: From any state with `S = 0`, ANY valid move MUST change `S` to a non-zero value.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Nim-Sum Winning Move for Piles [3, 4, 5]

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes exact pile reduction required to guarantee a win.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding the explicit winning move in a Game of Nim.
wAnswers.whereUsed: AI game agents, optimal move generation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) search for target pile with x_i ^ S < x_i.

algorithms.title: Grundy Numbers & Mex Function
algorithms.summary: Calculates Grundy values using Minimum Excluded Value (Mex) function to measure state advantage.
explanation: 1. Mex Function: `Mex(Set)` returns the smallest non-negative integer NOT present in `Set` (e.g. `Mex({0, 1, 3}) = 2`).
2. Grundy Number `G(u)`: `G(u) = Mex({ G(v) | v is reachable from u in 1 move })`.
3. Terminal Position: `G(terminal) = Mex({}) = 0`.
4. Interpretation: A state `u` is a Losing State iff `G(u) == 0`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Mex and Grundy numbers for subtraction game {1, 2, 3}

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes exact Grundy value of any game state using Mex reduction.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When evaluating non-standard impartial game components.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(1) set mex lookups after DP precomputation.

algorithms.title: Sprague-Grundy Theorem (Combining Sub-games)
algorithms.summary: Proves any impartial game is equivalent to a Nim pile of size G(u), allowing independent sub-games to be combined via XOR sum.
explanation: 1. Theorem: Every impartial game under normal play is equivalent to a Nim pile of size equal to its Grundy number `G(u)`.
2. Multi-Component Games: If a game consists of independent sub-games `G1, G2, ..., Gk`, the overall game's Grundy value is `G_total = G1 ^ G2 ^ ... ^ Gk`.
3. Winning Criterion: First player wins iff `G_total != 0`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace 3 independent sub-games with Grundy values G1=3, G2=5, G3=6
traceSteps: G_total == 0 -> Losing state for current player!

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines complex composite impartial games into a single Nim-Sum evaluation.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When a game splits into multiple independent sub-games.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Chess endgame piece simplification, multi-pile custom move games.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces exponential joint state exploration with independent sub-game XOR summation.

algorithms.title: Minimax Algorithm
algorithms.summary: Adversarial game-tree search algorithm maximizing agent score assuming opponent minimizes it.
explanation: 1. Maximizer Node: Chooses the child move that yields maximum value `max(child_values)`.
2. Minimizer Node: Chooses the child move that yields minimum value `min(child_values)`.
3. Leaf Evaluation: Evaluates board state utility value when depth limit is reached or terminal node found.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Depth 2 Minimax Tree
traceSteps: Root (Maximizer): Evaluates left child (Minimizer) and right child (Minimizer).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes optimal strategy in zero-sum two-player deterministic games.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When creating AI opponents for turn-based games like Tic-Tac-Toe, Checkers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Guarantees best possible outcome against optimal opponent.

algorithms.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning Optimization
algorithms.summary: Prunes subtrees in Minimax game search tree using Alpha (max lower bound) and Beta (min upper bound) cutoff threshold comparison.
explanation: 1. Alpha: The best score the Maximizer player is currently guaranteed at or above this level.
2. Beta: The best score the Minimizer player is currently guaranteed at or below this level.
3. Pruning Condition: If `beta <= alpha`, the current branch cannot affect the final decision. Prune remaining sibling branches immediately.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Alpha-Beta Pruning Cutoff
traceSteps: Maximizer evaluates left branch -> Score = 5. Alpha becomes 5.
Minimizer evaluates right branch's 1st child -> Score = 3.
Since Minimizer chooses <= 3 and Maximizer already has 5 on left, Beta = 3 <= Alpha = 5!

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Reduces game tree search nodes by up to 50% depth factor.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When searching deep game trees (Chess, Checkers, Go).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Stockfish, Deep Blue, modern game tree search engines.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Prunes unpromising subtrees without affecting the final minimax decision.
